content: The treatment for vaginitis depends on the underlying cause of the infection. It may involve oral or topical antibiotics, antifungal creams, antibacterial creams, or similar medications. Cortisone-containing creams can be used to alleviate irritation, and antihistamines may be prescribed if an allergic reaction is present. For postmenopausal women experiencing irritation and inflammation due to low estrogen levels, topical estrogen creams may be recommended. Medical Therapy for Vaginitis Treatment is advised for women presenting with symptoms. The primary goal of therapy in nonpregnant women is to alleviate vaginal symptoms and signs of infection. Additional benefits may include reducing the risk of acquiring sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, HIV, and other viral STDs. When selecting a treatment regimen, healthcare providers should consider patient preferences, potential side effects, drug interactions, and any coexisting infections. Women undergoing treatment should avoid sexual intercourse or use condoms consistently and correctly. Douching is discouraged as it may increase the risk of relapse, and there is no evidence supporting its use for symptom relief or treatment. Follow-Up for Vaginitis Follow-up visits are unnecessary if symptoms resolve. However, recurrence of bacterial vaginosis (BV) is common. Women should be advised to return for evaluation if symptoms recur. The detection of certain BV-associated organisms may indicate antimicrobial resistance and influence the risk of treatment failure. In cases of recurrence, alternative treatment regimens may be considered, though re-treatment with the same topical regimen is also acceptable during early recurrence. Monthly oral metronidazole combined with fluconazole has been evaluated as a suppressive therapy. Management of Sexual Partners in BV Clinical trials suggest that treating a woman’s sexual partner(s) does not affect her response to therapy or the likelihood of recurrence. Therefore, routine treatment of sexual partners is not recommended. Special Considerations for BV Allergy or Intolerance to Recommended Therapy: Intravaginal clindamycin cream is preferred for women allergic to or intolerant of metronidazole or tinidazole. Intravaginal metronidazole gel may be an option for those who cannot tolerate systemic metronidazole but should not be used in women allergic to metronidazole. Pregnancy: Treatment is recommended for all pregnant women with symptoms of BV. While BV is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes such as preterm labor, preterm birth, and postpartum endometritis, the primary benefit of treatment is symptom relief. Additional potential benefits include reducing the risk of infectious complications during pregnancy and lowering the risk of other infections, including STDs and HIV. Trichomoniasis Topical antimicrobials, such as metronidazole gel, are not recommended for treating trichomoniasis as they do not achieve therapeutic levels in the urethra or perivaginal glands. Other topical antimicrobials have been used occasionally but are unlikely to be more effective than metronidazole gel. Follow-Up for Trichomoniasis Reinfection rates are high among patients diagnosed with trichomoniasis, with 17% reinfected within three months in one study. Rescreening for Trichomonas vaginalis at three months is recommended for sexually active women. Rescreening is not advised for men. Most recurrent infections result from sexual contact with untreated partners, though some cases may involve reduced susceptibility to metronidazole. Management of Sexual Partners in Trichomoniasis Sexual partners of patients with trichomoniasis should be treated. Patients should abstain from sexual activity until both they and their partners have completed therapy and are asymptomatic. Male partners should be treated with either a single 2 g dose of tinidazole or 500 mg of metronidazole taken orally twice daily for seven days. Special Considerations for Trichomoniasis Allergy, Intolerance, and Adverse Reactions: Patients with immediate-type allergies to nitroimidazoles (e.g., metronidazole, tinidazole) may undergo desensitization under specialist supervision. Topical therapies with non-nitroimidazole drugs can be attempted, but cure rates are low (<50%). Pregnancy: Trichomoniasis during pregnancy is associated with adverse outcomes such as preterm delivery and low birth weight. While metronidazole treatment does not reduce perinatal morbidity, it may relieve symptoms and prevent neonatal respiratory or genital infections. Breastfeeding women treated with metronidazole should withhold breastfeeding during treatment and for 12–24 hours after the last dose. For tinidazole, breastfeeding should be interrupted during treatment and for three days after the last dose. HIV Infection: T. vaginalis infection in HIV-positive women may increase genital shedding of HIV, enhancing transmission. Treatment for trichomoniasis has been shown to reduce HIV shedding. HIV-positive women should be screened for trichomoniasis upon entry into care and at least annually thereafter. Rescreening three months after therapy is recommended due to the high recurrence rate. A multi-dose regimen of metronidazole (500 mg twice daily for seven days) may be considered for HIV-positive women. Vulvovaginal Candidiasis (VVC) Follow-up visits are only necessary if symptoms persist or recur within two months of initial onset. Management of Sexual Partners in VVC VVC is not typically transmitted sexually, and there is no evidence supporting the treatment of sexual partners. However, male partners with balanitis (characterized by erythema, pruritus, or irritation of the glans penis) may benefit from topical antifungal treatment. Special Considerations for VVC Allergy, Intolerance, and Adverse Reactions: Topical antifungal agents rarely cause systemic side effects but may cause local irritation or burning. Oral antifungal agents can occasionally cause nausea, abdominal pain, or headache. Rarely, oral azoles may lead to elevated liver enzymes or interact with other medications, such as warfarin, calcium channel blockers, and protease inhibitors. Complicated VVC: Recurrent VVC (RVVC), defined as four or more symptomatic episodes in one year, affects less than 5% of women. Vaginal cultures should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis and identify non-albicans species, such as Candida glabrata, which are less responsive to conventional therapies. Treatment for RVVC caused by C. albicans includes short-duration oral or topical azole therapy, followed by maintenance regimens such as weekly oral fluconazole for six months. For non-albicans VVC, longer therapy durations or boric acid capsules (600 mg vaginally for two weeks) may be effective. Severe VVC: Pregnancy: Only topical azole therapies applied for seven days are recommended during pregnancy. HIV Infection: HIV-positive women have higher rates of vaginal Candida colonization and symptomatic VVC, correlating with immunosuppression severity. Treatment for VVC in HIV-positive women is similar to that for seronegative women. Long-term prophylaxis with fluconazole (200 mg weekly) is effective but not routinely recommended.
